This person is a 42-year-old former North Sea oil rig electrician from Aberdeen who supports net zero only if the implementation includes a legally backed Just Transition Deal: fully funded retraining vouchers tied to high-wage offshore wind and CCUS jobs in the same region, local content requirements in CfD rounds, and wage bridges so he can pay his mortgage while reskilling.

This person is a 38-year-old HM Treasury economist in London who argues for a technology-neutral implementation: a steadily rising, economy-wide carbon price with border adjustments and a household dividend, competitive auctions without local content rules, and sunset clauses on subsidies to avoid locking in inefficient spending.

This person is a 29-year-old low-income private renter in Manchester, a single mother, who wants implementation to mandate minimum EPC C for rentals by 2028, offer landlord-targeted grants contingent on rent-freeze clauses, and require heat pump–ready wiring so her bills drop without her being priced out.

This person is a 62-year-old small buy-to-let landlord in Leeds who accepts efficiency upgrades but demands phased EPC deadlines by property type, 100% capital allowances for insulation and heat pumps, low-interest green mortgages, and an appeals process for hard-to-treat terraces.

This person is a 55-year-old Welsh upland sheep farmer near Brecon who supports net zero if agricultural methane is handled via incentives not taxes: long-term ELMs contracts with clear payment rates for peat restoration and hedgerows, grants for anaerobic digesters, and exemptions for small herds during drought years.

This person is a 34-year-old conservation NGO policy lead in Bristol who wants implementation to integrate climate and nature: spatial planning that prioritizes onshore wind and solar on low-biodiversity sites, mandatory biodiversity net gain for all energy projects, and redirecting ELMs toward results-based habitat outcomes with transparent monitoring.

This person is a 45-year-old National Grid connections manager based in Reading who insists the 2050 goal requires reforms: first-ready-first-served queue management, anticipatory investment allowances from Ofgem, statutory 12-month planning timelines for new 400kV lines, and standardised curtailment rules for batteries.

This person is a 68-year-old parish council chair in rural Norfolk who will oppose pylons unless implementation guarantees community benefits: mandatory undergrounding near villages and heritage sites, compulsion for developers to fund local energy rebates, and enforceable construction noise limits.

This person is a 35-year-old disabled commuter in London who backs zero-emission transport if implementation prioritizes accessibility: a national ZEBRA-style fund tied to ramp reliability metrics, retaining some curbside parking for Blue Badge users, and ring-fencing road-pricing revenue to freeze bus and Tube fares.

This person is a 47-year-old Midlands logistics SME owner with 20 diesel vans who wants a practical phase-in: grants for electric vans and depot chargers, priority grid connections for freight depots, interoperable public chargers on motorways, and temporary exemptions or e-fuel credits in Clean Air Zones until 2030.

This person is a project manager for offshore wind based in Aberdeen in his 40s who wants the UK to hit net zero by 2050 by fixing Contracts for Difference design (realistic strike prices and indexation), speeding marine planning and leasing decisions, investing in port infrastructure, and reforming the grid connection queue and offshore transmission to enable multi-purpose interconnectors, because delays have already sunk projects he worked on and threaten local jobs.

This person is a Cornish inshore fisher in her 50s who supports climate action but demands that offshore wind rollout include co-designed siting to protect spawning grounds, mandatory cable burial depths and transit corridors, compensation for gear loss, and a binding community benefits fund, because she has already lost income to poorly planned marine developments.

This person is a gas boiler engineer from Leeds in his 30s who argues the implementation should avoid cliff-edge bans and instead sequence the transition with clear, realistic phase-out dates, funded retraining, clarity on hydrogen’s role, allowance for hybrid heat pumps in hard-to-insulate homes, and robust consumer protections and warranties, because sudden rules could strand his skills and leave customers without affordable options.

This person is a retrofit coordinator and heat pump installer in Birmingham in her late 20s who wants a stable decade-long Boiler Upgrade Scheme with higher grants for social housing, heat pump–ready building regulations for all new builds from 2025, simplified MCS/PAS paperwork, and DNO-backed street-by-street upgrades so she can scale her business and cut bills for low-income clients.

This person is a Treasury economist in London in his 50s who supports net zero if delivered through a clear carbon pricing pathway (tightening the UK ETS cap and extending it judiciously to sectors like domestic maritime), a UK carbon border adjustment to protect industry, and revenue recycling via NIC cuts or lump-sum rebates to offset regressive impacts, because he is accountable for fiscal stability and public consent.

This person is a low-income private renter and single mother in Hull in her early 30s who wants the policy to reinstate and enforce Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards to EPC C for landlords with grant support, introduce a social energy tariff, and ban rent hikes tied to subsidy-funded upgrades, because high bills and a cold, damp home are harming her child’s health.

This person is a National Grid system planner based near Warwick in his mid-40s who argues for anticipatory investment and a strategic spatial energy plan, faster consent for new high-voltage lines (targeting one-year decisions), transparent connection queue reform, and OFGEM allowances for early grid build, because decade-long lead times make 2050 targets unattainable.

This person is a Somerset parish councillor and countryside campaigner in her 60s who insists that new transmission and wind projects include undergrounding in sensitive landscapes, generous community benefits and bill discounts, design codes to reduce visual impact, and meaningful consultation with route alternatives, because she has seen trust collapse after top-down pylon decisions.

This person is a manager in airline operations at Heathrow in his late 30s who wants the transition to prioritize a UK sustainable aviation fuel mandate with price support (such as contracts for difference), airspace modernization and efficiency standards, and coordination with CORSIA rather than unilateral tax hikes that could shift traffic, because he must keep routes viable while decarbonising.

This person is a rail transport planner and passenger advocate in Greater Manchester in her mid-30s who argues the policy should fund a rolling electrification program, restore and expand canceled HS2 and Northern Powerhouse Rail capacity, integrate fares and ticketing, and rebalance taxes to discourage short‑haul flights where rail is competitive, because modal shift is the fastest way to cut transport emissions.

This person is a 42-year-old offshore wind project finance director in Aberdeen who wants the UK to hit net zero by accelerating delivery: statutory 12-month offshore consent timelines, coordinated offshore transmission (not radial spaghetti), anticipatory grid investment, and predictable Contracts for Difference with supply-chain sustainability criteria. They push for faster marine spatial planning that balances habitats protection with clear leasing maps, port upgrade funds for nacelle and blade manufacturing, and a stable carbon price floor to underpin investment. They care because they have seen deals stall over grid connection queues and planning uncertainty that drive up consumer costs and risk the UK losing projects to the EU.

This person is a 55-year-old trawler captain out of Grimsby who supports net zero but demands marine policies that do not crush fishing livelihoods: binding requirements for fishing corridors through wind arrays, cumulative impact assessments across projects (not site-by-site), and a statutory compensation and gear-adaptation fund paid from offshore wind revenues. They want seasonal rather than permanent closures where possible, co-designed monitoring with fishermen on board, and rules to site cables away from key grounds. They care because their catches and safety have already been affected by poorly marked infrastructure and piecemeal planning.

This person is a 50-year-old gas boiler installer who runs a six-person SME in Bradford and wants a practical, staged heat transition: a clear end date for new gas-only boilers paired with a guaranteed five-year training voucher scheme, recognition of hybrid heat pumps for hard-to-insulate homes, and simplified certification (reduce MCS paperwork) without compromising quality. They argue for rebalancing levies off electricity so heat pumps are cheaper to run, EPC reform to reflect low-temperature systems, and grant eligibility for small landlords and social housing so their order book does not vanish overnight. They care because rushed bans and cheap unqualified competitors could sink their family business.

This person is a 33-year-old product manager at a UK heat pump manufacturer in Bristol who wants firm signals: a 2033 end date for gas boiler sales, heat-pump-ready standards in all new builds by 2026, scaled Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants with top-ups for off-gas rural homes, and streamlined permitted development for external units. They push for electricity/gas price rebalancing by shifting policy costs to general taxation, mass procurement to cut unit costs, and local training academies to expand the qualified workforce. They care because predictable demand lets them invest in UK assembly lines and bring down costs for households.

This person is a 29-year-old low-income renter in Tottenham on a prepayment meter who supports net zero but demands it not be funded regressively: move policy levies from electricity bills to progressive taxation, cap standing charges, and ban forced prepayment switches. They want minimum energy efficiency standards to EPC C for rentals with deadlines that trigger landlord grants, paired with rent-rise caps to prevent displacement. They advocate area-based retrofits with trusted local installers, Heat Network tariff protections, and a one-stop shop to actually navigate grants. They care because their cold, damp flat is expensive to heat and past schemes never reached them.

This person is a 47-year-old local authority housing decarbonisation officer in Greater Manchester who wants multi-year, devolved funding and realistic delivery rules: 10-year capital settlements for area-based retrofits, flexibility in PAS 2035 for solid-wall terraces, and data sharing from energy suppliers to target fuel poverty. They ask for enforcement teeth on landlord standards, a property MOT to track upgrades at sale or let, and permitted development for external wall insulation and air-source heat pumps. They care because stop-start grants and rigid rules strand projects mid-street and waste scarce council capacity.

This person is a 44-year-old union convenor at the Port Talbot steelworks who backs net zero if it protects good jobs: a bespoke contract-for-difference for low-carbon steel, a UK carbon border adjustment to stop dirty imports, and funded pilots for hydrogen DRI or EAF with guaranteed affordable power. They want just transition deals covering retraining, wage protection during retooling, and worker voice in tech choices, plus green public procurement for low-embodied-carbon steel in HS2 and housing. They care because their members cannot gamble mortgages on policy vagueness or a sudden furnace shutdown.

This person is a 26-year-old climate justice and circular economy researcher in London who opposes locking in fossil infrastructure and wants demand-side policy first: mandatory product standards and material passports to cut steel use, recycled-content requirements, and green public procurement to drive scrap-based EAF over CCS on blast furnaces. They support a CBAM tied to climate finance for developing countries, no public subsidies for fossil CCS outside hard-to-abate residuals, and timelines to halve industrial emissions by 2035. They care because they see CCS overuse as delaying real change and shifting costs to future taxpayers.

This person is a 61-year-old Welsh hill farmer in Powys who accepts net zero but insists on viable land policies: ELMS payments that reward hedgerows, peat protection, and agroforestry without blanket conifer planting on productive pasture; recognition of stable methane (GWP*) to set fair livestock targets; grants for slurry covers and methane inhibitors; and on-farm solar and small anaerobic digestion with quick grid connections. They want border standards so food imports meet UK environmental rules. They care because one-size-fits-all tree targets threaten their family farm and Welsh-speaking community.

This person is a 40-year-old director of a rewilding NGO in the Scottish Highlands who wants nature-based solutions embedded in net zero: legally binding nature targets alongside the carbon budget, large-scale peatland and saltmarsh restoration with rigorous MRV, and public-private blended finance with strong additionality tests for carbon credits. They urge limits on bioenergy with carbon capture to true residues, biodiversity net gain extended offshore, and long-term tenure security for landscape projects plus community benefit funds. They care because restoring ecosystems can sequester carbon and cut flood risk more cheaply than engineered fixes if policy stops subsidising perverse land uses.
